body: Global technology giants are pouring unprecedented capital into Southeast Asia, framing the region as the indisputable epicenter of the artificial intelligence boom. The headline figures are staggering: Amazon Web Services has consolidated a regional commitment exceeding $33 billion through 2039, Microsoft has pledged $2.2 billion in Malaysia and $2.5 billion in Indonesia, Google has unrolled a $2 billion deployment, and Nvidia has partnered with YTL Power in a $2.36 billion AI venture in Johor. Regional governments have eagerly embraced this influx, celebrating every new hyper-scale data center as validation of their digital transformation agendas.

Yet beneath this celebratory narrative lies a troubling geoeconomic asymmetry. The surge in foreign direct investment into Southeast Asian compute infrastructure replicates the structural logic of a classic extractive economy, a modern digital plantation.

A rigorous examination of local Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) reveals the mechanics of this value leakage.

The vast majority of capital expenditures announced by foreign hyperscalers does not circulate within host economies. Capital flows directly out of the region to purchase high-end graphics processing units (GPUs), specialized servers, and advanced liquid-cooling systems manufactured abroad.

What remains on local balance sheets is largely confined to low-margin civil construction, site maintenance, and basic utility bills. Concurrently, effective corporate tax receipts are hollowed out by aggressive tax holidays granted by competing investment boards.

Southeast Asia thus finds itself caught in a structural trap. The region imports hyper-expensive hardware, consumes its own finite natural resources to run intensive computational workloads, and then buys back proprietary software and fine-tuned AI applications at high subscription rates. Without a fundamental pivot in regional policy, this digital expansion will entrench a relation of technological vassalage rather than foster genuine economic leapfrogging.
The Resource Trap and the Race to the Bottom

The resulting ecological burden is severe. AI computational workloads require unprecedented energy density, with power requirements per rack surging from 8 kilowatts in 2021 to over 30 to 80 kilowatts for advanced model training. In Malaysia, where the data center pipeline stands at 2.4 gigawatts, sector power consumption is projected to exceed 5,000 megawatts by 2035, consuming up to 40 percent of Peninsular Malaysia’s current capacity.
Across ASEAN, data center electricity demand will jump from 9 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 68 terawatt-hours by 2030, straining power grids heavily reliant on fossil fuels.

Equally acute is the strain on regional hydrology. Evaporative cooling systems for a standard 100-megawatt data center facility devour roughly 4.2 million liters of water daily, an extraction volume equivalent to the daily domestic consumption of hundreds of thousands of local residents. Host governments are left to fund the secondary infrastructure required to sustain these facilities, effectively socializing environmental costs while private foreign entities privatize the economic rents.
